metadata.title: Australia defends under-16 social media ban despite widespread use

content.text:
Investing.com -- Australia's government defended its ban on social media use by children under 16 after regulatory data showed that more than eight in ten teenagers remained active on social platforms three months after the restrictions took effect.
Australia introduced the world-first ban on December 10, citing concerns about social media's effects on children's mental and physical health. The policy is being closely watched by other governments and has faced criticism from major technology companies, many of which are based in the U.S.
Andrew Leigh, Australia's assistant minister for productivity, competition, charities and treasury, said the restrictions had changed conversations among parents and led to the closure of millions of accounts.
Leigh acknowledged that the government never expected full compliance, comparing the policy with minimum drinking-age laws, which remain in place despite violations.
Data from Australia's eSafety regulator showed that children aged 10 to 15 were using social media in March at roughly the same frequency as before the ban took effect.
The study also found that parents had become less aware of their children's online activity, illustrating the difficulty of enforcing age restrictions across widely used digital services.
The findings were broadly consistent with preliminary figures released by eSafety in March.
Australia's centre-left Labor government has since proposed tougher enforcement measures, including doubling the maximum penalty that can be imposed on technology companies that fail to comply with the restrictions.
The policy places responsibility on social media platforms to prevent underage users from maintaining accounts rather than penalising children or their parents directly.
